background.definition: Constipation is a subjective complaint of straining, decreased frequency, and/or decreased volume of bowel movements. A normal frequency of bowel movements ranges from three times a day to three times a week.

list.listitem: Constipation results in more than 100,000 hospitalizations/year.
Various sources suggest that constipation generates between 2.5 and 6.0 million office visits annually.
Incidence varies by geographic region, and is more common in the upper Midwest, Maine, Alaska, and Vermont.
Very few studies exist regarding incidence. One study showed an incidence of 40 cases/1000 among Caucasians.
Incidence increases with age and is higher in women than in men.
Incidence after hemorrhagic stroke is 66% and after ischemic stroke is 51%.
Fifteen percent of the adult population has symptoms of constipation each year.
With the increase in use of opioids chronically there is a marked increase in constipation ranging from 22% to 81%.
In patients who self report constipation, 94% of patients meet ROME IV criteria for functional constipation criteria.
More than $800 million is spent on laxatives per year in the United States.
Tertiary care evaluation for constipation is reported on average to cost $2752/patient.
Causes of constipation are shown in the Differential Diagnosis table. It is often idiopathic.
Prescription or OTC medications frequently cause constipation (see ).
Inactivity.
Decreased colonic motility can cause constipation.
Changes in stool consistency due to low-fiber diet or decreased fluid intake can cause constipation.
Change in stool caliber due to a stricture can cause constipation.
Hormonal imbalance.

Disordered defecation is associated with a feeling of incomplete evacuation, a feeling of obstruction, and need to digitally manipulate to remove stool, while slow transit constipation is associated with infrequent bowel movements and abdominal bloating.B
Consider testing CBC, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, calcium, glucose, and thyroid stimulating hormone if symptoms persist despite conservative treatment. B
Colonoscopy should be performed on patients with red flag symptoms. A
Anorectal physiology and colon transit time investigations may help to identify the underlying etiology and improve the outcome in patients with refractory constipation. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Chronic, intermittent changes in bowel habits; no obvious pathology found on exam
Anal pain on defecation; blood on toilet paper; positive anoscopy
Persistent pain, tenderness and/or swelling in anal area; positive anoscopy
In most cases, hair loss, dry skin, etc.
History of progressive renal disease; elevated serum BUN
Usually elderly patient with cogwheeling and resting tremor on neuro exam
Neurological symptoms on exam suggesting MS
Early history of constipation as a child or adolescent; classic barium enema findings
Physical exam will suggest stigmata of scleroderma
Physical exam will denote spinal cord injury
Vaginal delivery; rectocoele on pelvic exam

list.listitem: Rome II criteria, an expert international consensus guide for diagnosing chronic functional constipation, are shown in .
Patients may complain of infrequent bowel movements, abdominal distention/bloating, incomplete evacuation, straining, and/or passing hard stool.

Ask about warning/alarm signs: significant weight loss, rectal bleeding and/or pain, abdominal distention and/or pain, nausea and/or vomiting, and melena. Patients with these findings should generally have colonoscopy.
Disordered defecation is associated with a feeling of incomplete evacuation, a feeling of obstruction, and need to digitally manipulate to remove stool.
Slow transit constipation is associated with infrequent bowel movements and abdominal bloating.
The physical exam may reveal abdominal distention and/or masses, and sometimes hard stool in the rectal vault.

Patients should undergo fecal occult blood testing at the initial visit. If the history and physical exam do not suggest warning signs for systemic or structural abnormalities, additional testing may not be warranted unless the patient does not respond to treatment.
If the patient does not respond to treatment, consider checking CBC, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, calcium, glucose, and thyroid stimulating hormone.

Colonoscopy should be performed if the patient has any red flags, is anemic, has a positive fecal occult blood test, or has a family history of colon cancer. Alternative testing would be a double contrast barium enema and flexible sigmoidoscopy. It should also be performed if the patient is over 50 years of age and has not had recent colonoscopy.
Digital rectal exam has high sensitivity (93.2%), specificity (58.7%) and predictive value (91%) in diagnosing anorectal dyssynergia at the bedside.

In patients whose primary symptom is constipation, CT colonography may be an aceptable alternative to colonoscopy as an initial study due to higher precentage of incomplete colonoscopy studies due to poor prep and/or discomfort.
Anorectal physiology and colon transit time investigations may help identify the underlying etiology and improve the outcome in patients with refractory constipation.

A studty of twenty patients using a novel smartphone application using the Bristol Stool Scale (BSS) and other visual stool characteristics had high accuracy compared with the two expert gastroenterologists. Trained Artificial Intelligence was superior to subject self-reporting of BSS. AI assessments could provide more objective outcome measures for stool characterization
A clinical rule for distinguishing slow transit from rectal evacuatory constipation has been developed; it has not been prospectively validated.
Rome Criteria are useful for distinguishing patients with irritable bowel syndrome.
Take a careful history focusing on the onset of symptoms and possible etiologies, including a careful medication history.

Identify any warning/alarm signs such as acute onset (if not medication induced), significant weight loss, rectal bleeding and/or pain, abdominal distention and/or pain, nausea and/or vomiting, and melena. Patients with warning/alarm symptoms and those over age 50 without a recent study should be referred for colonoscopy.
Initial treatment is with bulk laxatives, fluids, exercise, and high fiber diet. Consider medication changes if they may be causing constipation.
For patients with chronic symptoms, consider IBS. Try above conservative therapy with addition of polyethylene glycol or bisacodyl, and referral if there is an inadequate response.

The initial management of symptomatic constipation is typically dietary modification, including a high-fiber diet, fluid supplementation and exercise. Discontinue offending medications, if possible. B
The osmotic laxative polyethylene glycol (PEG) and the stimulant senna are effective. [SORT A]

Psyllium, SupraFiber, magnesium salts, stimulants (bisacodyl and sodium picosulfate), fruit-based laxatives (kiwi, mango, prunes, and ficus), and yogurt with galacto-oligosaccharide/prunes/linseed oil are effective in many patients. [SORT B] ]
Polyethylene glycol and lubiprostone are effective for the management of chronic constipation. A
Bisacodyl is more effective than many prescription medications for chronic constipation (LOE 1A).
Treatment should be based on efficacy, tolerability, compliance as well as cost. C
In patients with defecatory disorders, more than 70% of patients treated through biofeedback for pelvic floor retraining improved their symptoms.A

For opioid induced constipation, traditional laxatives are recommended as first-line therapy, and if that is not effective then naldemedine 0.2 mg daily or naloxegol 12.5 to 25 mg daily are recommended.A

A systematic review of 41 studies concluded there is good evidence to recommend polyethylene glycol (PEG) or senna as first-line laxatives, and moderate evidence to support fiber supplements, fruits, stimulant laxatives, and magnesium-based products.

A systematic review found good evidence for polyethylene glycol (PEG) and the stimulant senna; moderate evidence for psyllium, magnesium salts, stimulants such as bisacodyl and sodium picosulfate, fruit-based laxatives, and yogurt with galacto-oligosaccharide/prunes/linseed oil; and insufficient evidence for polydextrose, inulin, and fructo-oligosaccharide.

American College of Gastroenerology guidelines (2023) recommend the use of chloride channel activators and guanylate cyclase activators to treat global IBS with constipation predominant symptoms. The same guidelines strongly recommend polyethylene glycol, sodium picosulfate, linaclotide, plecanatide, and prucalopride for treating chronic idiopathic constipation in adults, with conditional support for fiber, lactulose, senna, magnesium oxide, and lubiprostone, emphasizing evidence-based use and shared decision making.

Use polyethylene glycol (PEG) for the management of chronic constipation when dietary management is inadequate.An RCT with 239 patients with chronic constipation found that they were more likely to have a response with PEG (14.6-17.0 g/day) than tegaserod (50% vs 30%; NNT = 5).It has been studied for up to 6 months.

There is good limited evidence to recommend polyethylene glycol (PEG) or senna as first-line laxatives, and moderate evidence to support fiber supplements, fruits, stimulant laxatives, and magnesium-based products. A systemic review and meta-analysis of 21 RCTs indicate that bisacodyl (Dulcolax) is more effective than prescription medications that include prucalopride, lubiprostone, tegaserod (not available in US due to safety concerns), and sodium picosulfate in the number of spontaneous bowel movements per week in chronic idiopathic constipations .
The use of psyllium supplements and lactulose for the treatment of constipation is less effective than PEG and lubiprostone.
The evidence is inconclusive for using common agents, such as milk of magnesia, senna, magnesium hydroxide and stool softeners, for chronic constipation. They appear to be useful in some patients.

However, in a small double-blinded RCT of 90 patients with idiopathic chronic constipation (mean age, 42 years; 93% women; mean duration of symptoms, 9.9 years), senna 1 gram daily and magnesium oxide 1.5 grams daily were six times more effective than placebo for overall symptom improvement.
In chronic idiopathic constipation trials like many gastroentestinal function disorders has a placebo rate between 4-44% depending upon end points.
For patients with refractory fecal impaction, "Go-Lytely" was safe and effective in a small study with 10 patients.

For patients with irritable bowel syndrome, a recent systematic review concluded that the use of bulking agents (e.g., fiber supplements) failed to improve abdominal pain or overall relief of IBS symptoms.
After urogyncological surgery, adding PEG3350 postoperatively in addition to docusate sodium routine, did not reduce time to first bowel movement.

A meta-analysis of nine RCTs found that lubiprostone is a safe and effective drug in the treatment of chronic idiopathic constipation and irritable bowel syndrome with constipation with limited adverse effects at 3-month follow-up.

Linaclotide, an intestinal secretogogue,was helpful in two 12-week trials to treat chronic idiopathic constipation and IBS-C. An additional trial showed reduced abdominal symptoms of bloating, discomfort and pain.
In patients with chronic idiopathic constipation prucalopride has modest improvement in moderate to severe bloating symptoms compared to placebo - prucalopride (62.1%) vs placebo (49.6%).
Tegaserod is effective for constipation predominant irritable bowel but the cost is high. It was withdrawn by the FDA in 2007 from the US market due to concerns regarding cardiovascular safety.

Minesapride is a 5-HT4 receptor agonist that is an investigational treatment for irritable bowel syndrome with predominant constipation (IBS-C). It was no more effective than placebo in affecting the composite outcome of reducing abdominal pain and increasing spontaneous bowel movements in patients with severe symptoms.
Colchicine 0.6 mg PO TID is an effective treatment for idiopathic constipation in women (n = 16/16) or in severe constipation in developmentally impaired patients (n = 8/11).
Aprepitant triple therapy effective in preventing chemotherapy induced nausea and vomiting and signficantly reduces the risk of constipation but increases the risk of hiccups.
Tenapanor 50 mg given twice a day was found to be effective in treating IBS-C with improvement in abdominal pain and constipation. It is a sodium/hydrogen exchanger 3 (NHE3) agonist in small bowel.
For opioid-induced constipation (OIC), methylnaltrexone use is effective and safe in hospice patients for up to 6 months.

There was moderate‐certainty evidence that naldemedine taken orally improved bowel function within two weeks in adults with cancer and opioid‐induced bowel dysfunction but increased the risk of side effects, and that methylnaltrexone taken as an injection improved bowel function over two weeks in people receiving palliative care. The results of this review need to be interpreted with caution as they were not obtained from evidence that was of high‐certainty.

A Cochrane review on mu-opioid antagonists (MOA) for opioid-induced bowel dysfunction (OIBD) concluded that naldemedine improves bowel function over several weeks in people with cancer and OIBD but increases the risk of adverse (such as diarrhea) and did not change pain relief.

In a 12-week trial of 431 patients with OIC due to non-methadone opioid use, lubiprostone was associated with a 27.1% spontaneous bowel movement response rate compared to 18.9% in placebo treated patients (NNT = 12).
In a 12-week trial, naloxegol (25 mg/day) compared to placebo was associated with a higher response rate (i.e. more spontaneous bowl movements) in patients with OIC.

A meta-analysis determined that oral naloxone (naloxegol) (typically dosed in a range of 5 mg to 20 mg) sustained-release preparation daily, or in a 2:1 ratio of oxycodone to naloxone) is the safest and most effective treatment for opioid-induced constipation (OIC), although oral naloxone alone is not available in the United States as of this writing (June 2019). Naldemedine and alvimopan were also effective and safe.
In patients with opioid induced constipation, almost equal number of patients prefer either naloxegol (50.4%) or PEG3350 (48.0%). Both medications appear safe. Naloxegol is much more expensive.
Patients with refractory slow-transit constipation may benefit from total abdominal colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis.

Refractory slow-transit constipation associated with associated pelvic outlet obstruction may benefit from correction of the pelvic floor dysfunction and total abdominal colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis.

Sacral nerve stimulation (SNS) which is low voltage stimulation of the sacral nerve roots and is effective for fecal incontinence, but does not increase the frequency of bowel movements in patients with constipation.

Epidural anesthetics with or without opioids accelerates the return of gastrointestional mobility (high quality of evidence). Epidural containing a local anesthetic with the addition of an opioid decreases pain after abdominal surgery (moderate level of evidence). No difference seen in vomiting or gastrointestianl anastomosis leaks noted (low quality of evidence). Epidural anesthetics reduced the length of hospitalization for open surgery by almost one day (low quality of evidence).

Botox-A infiltration of the external anal sphincter (EAS) in incomplete motor spinal cord injury decreases the EAS contraction and the anal canal pressure during straining, and improves outlet constipation symptoms (n=16).

In the management of pelvic floor disorders, biofeedback may be effective, but no quality research studies currently support it. A systematic review identified 7 studies with 413 patients, but the studies were of poor quality. One study of 100 patients (96 female) notes it improved the quality of life at a cost $826 - $2369 per patient.
Prune juice is an effective and safe natural food therapy for chronic constipation

In this RCT (n=75), prunes, psyllum and kiwifruit were studied and compared. All three are efficious in treating constipation but kiwifruit was associated with the lowest rate of AEs and dissatisfaction with therapy.
Probiotics in one small study (n = 28) increased defecation frequency in elderly constipated patients by 24%. Controlled clinical trials of probiotics are scarce.
Comsumption of a fermented milk containing multiple probiotic strains and prebiotic fiber improved constipation in patients with Parkinson disease.
In patients with defecatory disorders, more than 70% of patients treated through biofeedback for pelvic floor retraining eleviated their symptoms (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence).

Gum chewing (commercially available sugarless gum for 15 minutes every 2 hours starting 2 hours postoperatively until first flatus is passed) after laparoscopic gynecologic surgery leads to earlier bowel motility and less need for postoperative narcotic analgesia. This simple intervention caused no apparent harm, had good acceptance by women, and has a negligible cost.
In RCT (n=52)Transcutaneous Electrical Acustimulation can improve constipation and symptoms of IBS by accelerating colon transit and reducing rectal sensation,

Electroaccupuncture, 28 half-hour sessions over an 8-week period, compared to sham accupuncture was more effective in producing at least 3 bowel movements per week in patients with <3 bowel movement per week. The effective of treatment continued for at least 3 months after treatment was discontinued.

Electroacupuncture is noninferior to prucalopride in relieving severe chronic constipation (24.91% vs 25.54%) with a good safety profile and less side effects. The effects of 8-week electroacupuncture was sustained for 24 weeks after treatment.

The initial management of symptomatic constipation is typically dietary modification, including a high-fiber diet and fluid supplementation. Recommend a daily fiber intake of 20 to 35 g daily with fluid supplementation to patients.
Increased physical activity seems to be helpful. Evidence is weak.
Discontinue offending medications if possible, and treat any underlying medical conditions that may be causing constipation.

Perineal self-massage, in addition to standard therapies (e.g., dietary fiber, use of stool softeners, increased exercise), significantly improves quality of life and measures of bowel function in patients with functional constipation.
Body position at the right height and knees higher than the floor while sitting on the commode may assist defecation in some patients.

In a study of 130 children with functional constipation, a constipation action plan (i.e., tailored instructions; red, yellow, and green zone symptoms; and maintenance and rescue medication doses) was similar to usual care (79% vs 82%) for symptom resolution.
Treatment for chronic constipation is life-long in many cases.
Hospitalization may be necessary in cases of severe constipation where the patient is dehydrated from anorexia, vomiting, and/or severe fecal impaction.
Rehydrate the patient.
Disimpact the patient with enemas or manual removal of stool.
For patients with refractory fecal impaction, "Go-Lytely" was safe and effective in a small study (n = 10/10).

In patients with chronic constipation, life-long management will be necessary to avoid severe constipation. Through the use of a high-fiber diet, adequate fluid ingestion, and medications such as polyethylene glycol, a patient should be able to have reasonably normal bowel movements. B

Patients should receive education on what constitutes a high-fiber diet, adequate fluid intake, the proper use of laxatives, avoidance of constipating OTC medications and foods, and increased physical activity. C

Minimal data exist regarding natural history, prognosis, or the effect on the quality of life. One study found a disappearance rate of 309/1000 person-years over 14.7 months. However, 89% with constipation noted no change in their symptoms over a period up to 20 months when resurveyed. B
Treatment in the elderly is based on empiric evidence. While studies found increased stool frequency with use of laxatives and stool softeners, the studies were poor quality.

No evidence based on five small studies that the laxatives lactulose, senna, co-danthramer combined with poloxamer, misrakasneham, docusate and magnesium hydroxide combined with liquid paraffin or combinations work any better than the other.

list.listitem: A small randomized trial of 89 patients demonstrated a trend that dexamethasone 6 to 16 mg given intravenously may resolve one episode of bowel obstruction with extremely low incidence of side effects (NNT = 6).
Dietary fiber in the form of wheat fiber or bran will help most pregnant women. Stimulant laxatives may work if a high-fiber diet is not effective.
See chapter on constipation in children.

feature.caption: Medication Classes Commonly Associated with Constipation.
Rome II Criteria for Chronic Constipation.
feature.feature_body: At least 12 weeks—which need not be consecutive—in the preceding 12 months of 2 or more of the following: Straining at least 25% of the time when defecating Lumpy or hard stools at least 25% of the time when defecating Sensation of incomplete evacuation at least 25% of the time when defecating Sensation of anorectal obstruction/blockage at least 25% of the time when defecating Manual maneuvers to facilitate defecation at least 25% of the time (e.g., digitgraal evacuation, support of the pelvic floor) Fewer than 3 defecations per week Loose stools are not present There are insufficient criteria for irritable bowel syndrome From Thompson EG, Longstreth GF, Drossman DA, et al. Functional bowel disorders and functional abdominal pain. Gut 1999;45:44.

feature.caption: Rome IV Criteria for Opioid-induced Constipation

tr.th: 1. New or worsening symptoms of constipation when initiating, changing or increasing opioid therapy that must include at least two or more items below:

tr.td: a. Straining during more than one-fourth (25%) of defecations
b. Lumpy or hard stools more than one-fourth (25%) of defecations
c. Sensation of incomplete emptying more than one-fourth (25%) of defecations
d. Sensation of anorectal obstruction/blockage more than one-fourth (25%) of defecations
e. Manual manuevers to faciltiate more than one-fourth (25%) of defecations (e.g. digital evacuations, support of pelvic floor)
f. Fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements per week

td.strong: 2. Loose stools are rarely present without use of laxatives
